questions.question: Define an element and explain why chemists needed to classify the elements. Describe the patterns noticed by Döbereiner and Newlands.
questions.expected_answer: An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom, which cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means. By the 1800s many elements were known and more were being discovered, each with different properties; classification groups elements with shared properties so that position tells you about each element and patterns can be found. Döbereiner (1829) found triads of three elements with similar properties, e.g. lithium, sodium, potassium or chlorine, bromine, iodine, where the middle atomic mass was roughly the average of the other two. Newlands (1865) arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and found that similar properties repeated every eighth element (law of octaves); it worked only for the lighter elements.

questions.question: Explain how Mendeleev constructed his Periodic Table in 1869, why he left gaps, and how the discovery of germanium supported his table. State how the modern table differs.
questions.expected_answer: Mendeleev arranged the 63 known elements in order of increasing atomic mass and placed elements with similar properties in the same column. Where the next element did not fit the properties of a column he left a gap, stating that an undiscovered element belonged there, and he predicted its properties from its neighbours. For eka-silicon he predicted atomic mass about 72 and density about 5.5 g/cm³; germanium, discovered in 1886, has atomic mass 72.6 and density 5.35 g/cm³, so the prediction was confirmed (gallium 1875 and scandium 1879 also matched). He also swapped tellurium and iodine to keep families together. The modern table is arranged by increasing atomic number (Moseley, 1913), which removes the need for such swaps; noble gases were added as Group 18.

questions.question: Describe the layout of the modern Periodic Table using the terms group, period, metals, non-metals and semi-metals. Give the group and period of chlorine, calcium and neon.
questions.expected_answer: Groups are the 18 vertical columns; elements in a group have similar chemical properties (Group 1 alkali metals, Group 17 halogens, Group 18 noble gases, Groups 3 to 12 transition metals). Periods are the 7 horizontal rows; properties change gradually from metals on the left to non-metals on the right. A staircase line from boron towards polonium and astatine separates metals (left and centre, more than three quarters of the elements) from non-metals (top right, plus hydrogen). Semi-metals lie along the staircase: boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium. Chlorine: Group 17, Period 3. Calcium: Group 2, Period 4. Neon: Group 18, Period 2.
